items.title: EFFECT OF AI-DRIVEN ADAPTIVE LEARNING PLATFORM ON SECONDARY SCHOOL STUDENTS' RETENTION IN CHEMISTRY IN ANAMBRA STATE
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the effect of an Artificial Intelligence-Driven Adaptive Learning Platform (AI-DALP) on secondary school students’ retention in Chemistry within the Onitsha Education Zone of Anambra State, Nigeria. The study specifically assessed the difference in delayed retention between students taught using AI-DALP and those taught using the Conventional Teaching Method (CTM) after controlling for immediate posttest performance, as well as whether retention differed by gender within the adaptive learning environment. Guided by two research questions and two null hypotheses tested at the 0.05 level of significance, the study adopted a quasi-experimental non-randomised pretest–posttest control-group design. The population comprised 548 Senior Secondary School II (SS2) Chemistry students across 22 public co-educational schools. Through purposive sampling based on ICT infrastructure availability, a sample of 59 students (30 in the AI-DALP group and 29 in the CTM group) was selected. The intervention lasted six weeks, covering Oxygen, Hydrogen, and Halogens, followed by a delayed retention test administered two weeks after the posttest. Data were collected using a 50-item Chemistry Achievement Test (CAT), validated by three experts, with an internal consistency reliability coefficient of 0.82 established using the Kuder–Richardson 20 (KR-20) formula. Data were analyzed using mean, standard deviation, and Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) with posttest scores as the covariate. The results indicated that students exposed to AI-DALP achieved significantly higher adjusted retention mean scores than those taught via CTM after controlling for posttest performance. Additionally, no statistically significant difference was observed in retention scores between male and female students taught using AI-DALP after accounting for posttest performance. The study concluded that AI-DALP effectively enhances durable Chemistry learning among secondary school students regardless of gender. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Adaptive Learning, Chemistry Education, Delayed Retention, Secondary Education, Gender, Onitsha Education Zone.

items.title: Effectiveness of an AI-Driven Early Warning System Integrated into Nursing Practice on Early Detection of Clinical Deterioration, Response Time, and Patient Safety Outcomes: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background: Clinical deterioration in hospitalized patients often precedes adverse events such as cardiac arrest, unplanned intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and mortality. While traditional early warning systems (EWS) based on vital signs have improved detection, their predictive accuracy and integration into nursing workflow remain suboptimal. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven systems leveraging nursing surveillance data may enhance early detection and response. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of an AI-driven early warning system integrated into nursing practice on early detection of clinical deterioration, nursing response time, and patient safety outcomes in adult medical-surgical wards. Methods: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial conducted across 12 medical-surgical units in two tertiary hospitals. Adult patients (N=4,286) were randomized to either the AI-driven EWS (intervention, n=2,143) or standard EWS care (control, n=2,143). The AI system analyzed nursing documentation patterns and vital signs in real time, generating risk scores displayed within the electronic health record. Primary outcomes included time to clinical deterioration detection, nursing response time to alerts, and composite patient safety outcomes (in-hospital mortality, unplanned ICU transfer, and cardiac arrest). Data were analyzed using intention-to-treat principles with mixed-effects models. Results: The AI-driven EWS significantly reduced time to deterioration detection (median 2.1 vs. 4.8 hours; p<0.001) and nursing response time (median 18 vs. 42 minutes; p < 0.001). The composite patient safety outcome occurred in 11.2% of intervention patients versus 16.8% of controls (adjusted odds ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.53-0.78; p<0.001). Unplanned ICU transfers were higher in the intervention group (24.9% increase; p=0.001), suggesting appropriate escalation. Conclusion: AI-driven EWS integrated into nursing practice substantially improved early detection, response time, and patient safety outcomes. These findings support implementation of AI-enhanced surveillance systems in acute care settings.

items.title: Effects of a self-regulated learning training on adolescents’ metacognitive awareness, learning processes and outcomes: a multi-method perspective
items.abstract: Abstract Adolescence represents an important developmental phase for self-regulated learning (SRL), marked by uneven growth in metacognitive knowledge, awareness, and regulatory skills. Research on supporting adolescents’ emerging SRL is particularly relevant in online learning environments (OLEs), where autonomous regulation is essential, but remains limited. This quasi-experimental field study examined immediate effects of a brief digital SRL training on secondary school students’ metacognitive awareness, learning outcomes, and regulatory processes during an online essay-writing task. The experimental group (EG; n = 37) received SRL training before the task, while a control group (CG; n = 32) received comparable training on ergonomics. Results showed significantly higher metacognitive awareness in the EG, but no effects on essay performance, domain-knowledge gains, or learning transfer. Process analyses revealed that the EG spent more time on task orientation, and prior domain knowledge (PK) moderated training effects on cognitive processes; in the EG, rereading and writing frequencies decreased with increasing PK, whereas they showed slight increases in the CG. Within-group associations showed more consistent positive links between PK and learning outcomes in the EG. Sequence analyses further suggested that successful EG students with different PK levels followed partly distinct regulatory pathways: high-PK students displayed metacognitive process sequences, whereas low-PK students relied more on planning-intensive mixed sequences. Overall, findings suggest that a brief SRL training can foster metacognitive awareness and selected regulatory behaviors, while highlighting the need for adaptive and temporally sensitive SRL support for adolescent learners. The study demonstrates the value of multi-method, process-oriented perspectives for informing future SRL intervention designs.

items.title: Effects of generative AI and translanguaging on second language writing complexity, accuracy, and fluency
items.abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) exhibits the potential to scaffold L2 students’ writing, research found that L2 students struggle to craft effective prompts for GenAI to produce high-quality feedback and responses. As such, there is a need to incorporate translanguaging into L2 students’ prompt engineering to capitalize on the learning potential of GenAI for L2 students. The present study, therefore, investigated whether the combined use of GenAI and translanguaging influenced L2 writing linguistic features. We adopted a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental design by assigning L2 writers to four groups: a control group, translanguaging - only, GenAI - only, and translanguaging + GenAI. Comparing the lexical complexity, syntactic complexity, accuracy, and fluency of the four groups, we found that GenAI had a significant positive impact on the lexical and syntactic complexity, accuracy, and fluency of L2 students’ writing, while translanguaging alone and the combination of GenAI and translanguaging did not yield significant positive impacts on most indices of the writing performance. L2 teachers are encouraged to integrate GenAI tools into writing instruction to improve students’ writing complexity, accuracy, and fluency, while providing scaffolding for translanguaging, as its benefits might not emerge automatically, particularly for advanced L2 writers.

items.title: Effects of Visual-Proprioceptive Integration of Hand Position on Immersive Experience and Performance
items.abstract: We investigated how visual–proprioceptive conflicts regarding perceived hand position alter sense of embodiment and our actions during head-mounted display (HMD) virtual reality (VR). Participants hit virtual objects with virtual mallets (training phase) while we manipulated the amount and type of virtual hand offset, the visibility of virtual hands, and the presence of vibration cues. The manipulations differentially affected reported presence, perceived body ownership, and sense of agency. To examine the aftereffects of this training, participants were subsequently asked to strike a stationary virtual target without any visual representation of virtual hands or mallets. Hand offset during training biased the direction, and increased the variability, of these test strikes. A follow-up extinction experiment found little sign of attenuation across five consecutive strikes. These findings suggest brief exposures to visual–proprioceptive conflicts can bias perception and action beyond the immediate training context.

items.title: Efficacy and Mechanism of Generative AI in Empowering English Writing Instruction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence technology brings new transformative opportunities to English writing instruction. This paper analyzes the efficacy and mechanism of generative AI in empowering English writing teaching. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model and Self-Regulated Learning theory, it summarizes teaching efficacy from three dimensions—the quality of writing output, cognitive support during the writing process, and real-time adaptation of writing feedback—and further reveals the underlying mechanism through three layers: cognitive load reduction, learning motivation activation, and metacognitive strategy activation. Using data from a 12-week quasi-experimental study, it compares the experimental and control groups in terms of writing performance, writing strategy use, and feedback engagement. The results show that generative AI-assisted instruction has a moderately strong facilitative effect on learners' writing performance, achieved mainly by reducing extraneous cognitive load, enhancing writing self-efficacy, and deepening feedback engagement. This study provides theoretical grounding and practical reference for integrating generative AI into the English writing classroom.

items.title: Embodied Education and Artificial Intelligence: an integrated pedagogical model for the design of hybrid, inclusive and reflective learning environments in secondary schools
items.abstract: This study analyses the integration of the embodied approach and artificial intelligence in educational contexts, investigating their effects on engagement, intrinsic motivation and school inclusion. The research, conducted at two upper secondary schools in the city of Naples, involved 180 students divided into an experimental group and a control group according to a quasi-experimental design. The experimental group took part in an 8-week educational intervention based on embodied activities, collaborative practices and guided use of generative artificial intelligence tools, whilst the control group followed traditional teaching activities. The study adopted a mixed-methods approach, integrating the Student Engagement Scale (SES), the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), semi-structured interviews and classroom observations. The results highlight a significant increase in engagement and intrinsic motivation within the experimental group, with preliminary positive indications also regarding the participation of students with special educational needs. The qualitative analysis further shows that AI-supported embodied activities fostered active participation, collaboration, multimodal accessibility and metacognitive reflection. Overall, the study suggests that the integration of embodied education and artificial intelligence, when supported by intentional pedagogical design, can contribute to the creation of more inclusive, reflective and participatory learning environments.

items.title: Empowering student-led climate solutions: the role of AI in STEAM education
items.abstract: This convergent mixed-methods study investigates the strategic integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into a university-level STEAM curriculum to empower students to design climate solutions. Combining quantitative survey data from 69 undergraduate students selected via a complete cohort census sampling approach (response rate: 84.1%) and multi-tiered purposive qualitative interviews with N = 25 participants ( N = 11 experts, N = 9 faculty members, and N = 5 student innovators), the findings indicate high technological familiarity and widespread adoption (100% AI tool use). Specifically, students reported the highest agreement for AI enhancing their creativity and learning independence (86.9%, M = 4.12), supporting their capacity to pivot from data collection to strategic solution design (73.9%, M = 3.78), and bolstering their perceived empowerment to propose climate solutions (76.8%, M = 3.84). Furthermore, self-reported student perceptions indicated that AI supported their critical thinking process (68.1%, M = 3.65), representing perceived cognitive scaffolding rather than an objective measure of skill performance. This supports the qualitative finding that AI acts as a “Complexity Mediator” in climate tasks. However, notable concerns were reported regarding accuracy (60.9%) and plagiarism (59.4%). To address this, the study proposes the AI-Empowered STEAM Climate Action Model (AISC-AM), a conceptual framework that structures STEAM as a Multi-Scalar Problem-Solving Ecosystem and mandates critical AI literacy and an “AI-in-the-Loop” validation structure. Informed by preliminary stakeholder appraisal, the proposed AISC-AM offers a structured pedagogical workflow to mitigate operational risks while connecting student-led research to regional climate policy platforms via youth organizational partnerships.

items.title: Ethnic Diversity, Organizational Diversity Climate, and the Perceived Value of Deepfake Personas: A User Study with Marketing Professionals
items.abstract: Beyond fraud, deepfake personas can be utilized in human-centered design to represent user groups. This study investigates how deepfake persona sets of different ethnic diversity can offer strategic value for human-computer interaction (HCI) design processes. In an online experiment with 81 marketing professionals evaluating persona sets of varying diversity, the more diverse sets were perceived as significantly more inclusive, more inspiring for market coverage, and more valuable for identifying market opportunities, with no compromise of perceived persona quality or task performance. Findings show that these perceived strategic benefits were consistently associated with organizational diversity climate, consistent with institutional theory. These findings advance persona, advertising, and HCI research by repositioning deepfake technology from a solely technological risk to a strategic design resource driven by the organizational diversity climate, with direct implications for inclusive HCI practice and diversity policies.

items.title: Examining the role of a structured AI-supported intervention in developing EFL students’ academic writing skills in Mozambican higher education
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping educational practices and redefining how academic writing is taught, learned, and assessed. This study explores the role of a structured AI-supported writing intervention on English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students’ academic writing performance and examines lecturers’ awareness of, and alignment with, emerging AI trends in a Mozambican public university. Employing an Exploratory Sequential Case Study-Mixed Methods design, data were collected through documents analyses, interviews, an intervention, and observations. Participants included eighteen undergraduate EFL students and five lecturers. Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Social Practice Theory (SPT), qualitative data were analysed thematically, while quantitative data were examined using descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test to measure performance differences. Findings revealed that students in the control group had limited informal exposure to AI and lacked ethical guidance, whereas students participating in the structured AI-supported intervention demonstrated higher levels of academic writing performance and responsible AI use following the intervention. However, most lecturers reported limited awareness of AI writing tools and students’ use of these technologies. From a TAM perspective, perceived usefulness, ease of use, and pedagogical support were associated with students’ acceptance of AI tools for academic writing purposes. The SPT interpretation further suggested that social interactions, supervision practices, and shared ethical norms contributed to how students integrated ChatGPT as an AI writing tool in their undergraduate writing practices. The study highlights the importance of AI literacy initiatives for both students and lecturers, as well as institutional ethical guidelines to support responsible and sustainable AI adoption in Mozambican higher education.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Computer Vision: A Comprehensive Study on Interpretability Techniques, and Applications
items.abstract: Abstract Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and medical image analysis. However, the opaque, black-box nature of these models limits their adoption in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, autonomous driving, and security, where accountability and trust are essential. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a critical research direction that seeks to make the decision-making process of deep models transparent and interpretable to human users without materially sacrificing predictive performance. While prior work has largely evaluated individual explainability techniques in isolation, few studies jointly deploy and quantitatively compare complementary explanation modalities within a single inference pipeline. We review recent literature published between 2023 and 2026, categorize explainability methods along the model-agnostic/model-specific and global/local dimensions, and provide a detailed technical analysis of five widely used techniques: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), Integrated Gradients, and saliency/attention-based maps. Building on this analysis, we propose an XAI-integrated computer vision framework that couples a fine-tuned Residual Network (ResNet-18) classifier with Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME explanation modules, and introduce an Explainability Consensus Score that quantifies the spatial agreement among the three explanation modalities for a given prediction. The framework is designed and specified for evaluation on the Chest X-ray Pneumonia dataset, with a complete evaluation protocol, planned performance metrics, and explainability-agreement metrics defined in advance of full experimental deployment; quantitative results will be reported following implementation and are intentionally not fabricated in this manuscript. Based on the reviewed literature and the qualitative behavior of the proposed explanation modules, we argue that combining local (SHAP, LIME) and gradient-based (Grad-CAM) explanations is expected to improve diagnostic transparency over any single technique used in isolation, a hypothesis the proposed Consensus Score is designed to test quantitatively. The paper concludes by discussing open challenges, including explanation faithfulness, computational overhead, bias propagation, and the evaluation of explainable vision transformers, and outlines future research directions toward standardized, responsible, and human-centered explainable computer vision systems. Keywords: Explainable Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision, Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Network, Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, Explainability Consensus Score, Model Interpretability, Trustworthy AI.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Zero-Day Cyberattack Detection in Healthcare: A Critical Review and an Integrated Framework for Clinical Cybersecurity
items.abstract: Healthcare delivery organisations have become preferred targets for cyber intrusion, and the clinical consequences of successful attacks now extend beyond information loss to measurable disruption of emergency, critical and diagnostic care. Signature-based defences cannot recognise previously unseen exploits, which has driven interest in machine learning detectors capable of identifying anomalous behaviour without prior knowledge of an attack pattern. Because such detectors are opaque, explainable artificial intelligence has been proposed as the mechanism through which their outputs can be audited, trusted and acted upon in clinical settings. This review examines whether that proposition is supported by the available evidence. Literature was identified through structured searching of open scholarly indexes, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching, and appraised for methodological adequacy, evidential strength and relevance to clinical deployment rather than for benchmark performance alone. The synthesis indicates that the two research streams have developed with limited contact. Work on detection of previously unseen attacks is dominated by retrospective evaluation on a small number of network datasets in which novelty is simulated by withholding labelled classes, a design that systematically flatters reported performance. Work on explanation is dominated by post-hoc feature attribution, whose faithfulness, stability and adversarial robustness remain contested, and which is poorly suited to characterising events that lie outside the training distribution. Healthcare-specific studies inherit both limitations while adding constraints related to medical device heterogeneity, data governance and clinical safety. Evidence that explanation improves analyst or clinician decision quality in security contexts is scarce, and current regulatory expectations for transparency are not matched by validated evaluation methods. An integrated framework is proposed that separates detection novelty, explanation target, explainee role and governance obligation as distinct design decisions, and that treats explanation quality as an empirical property requiring prospective human-centred evaluation rather than an assumed benefit.

items.title: Exploring Culturally Responsive Teaching Awareness in the Age of GenAI: Voices from Indonesian EFL Pre-Service Teachers
items.abstract: This study explores pre-service EFL teachers’ awareness of integrating GenAI into CRT in West Kalimantan, Indonesia. Using a qualitative descriptive design, data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 35 final-semester pre-service EFL teachers and analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis. Interview analysis reveals four interconnected dimensions of awareness: cognitive, pedagogical, critical/evaluative, and developmental. Participants recognized GenAI's limitations in representing local cultural knowledge, struggled to design culturally responsive prompts, and demonstrated the ability to identify cultural biases and inaccuracies in AI outputs. They also emphasized the need for practical training and institutional support to effectively integrate GenAI into culturally responsive learning. items.title: Fragmented Yet Concentrated: Primary-Study Overlap in Meta-Analyses on Generative AI in Education
items.abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses on learning with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have proliferated rapidly, but their number does not indicate whether they rest on distinct primary-publication bases or where synthesis production is concentrated. This tertiary study maps bibliographic overlap in 11 meta-analyses of quantitative learning effects indexed in the Education Resources Information Center (ERIC). A broader corpus of 24 ERIC-indexed reviews, including these 11 meta-analyses, provides descriptive context. Review-by-publication citation matrices were constructed, publication identities resolved, the corrected covered area (CCA) calculated, publication reuse examined, and the provenance of highly reused publications mapped. Across the 11 meta-analyses, 307 review-publication occurrences resolved to 197 unique publications. Most publications appeared in only one meta-analysis (141; 71.6%), but 13 appeared in at least four and one appeared in eight. The principal CCA was 5.58%, indicating low-to-moderate overlap at the slight/moderate boundary, and leave-one-review-out estimates ranged from 4.94% to 6.79%. The 24-review corpus had a CCA of 1.67%. Notably, all 11 first-author institutional affiliations were in Asia, including eight in mainland China, whereas the most frequently reused publications spanned four continents. The 11 meta-analyses therefore do not rest on wholly distinct publication bases, and their production is geographically concentrated. For evidence-informed decisions in open, distance and digital education, readers should assess not only the number of available syntheses but also the overlap and provenance of their publication bases. These conclusions concern bibliographic structure and institutional affiliation, not statistical dependence or the influence of individual publications on pooled estimates.

items.title: From Design to Discovery: A Systematic Review of Canva AI as a Pedagogical Tool in Education
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has drawn attention to digital learning tools that support creativity and effective teaching. Canva is originally a graphic design platform that evolved into an AI-assisted education tool. This study conducted a systematic review following the PRISMA guidelines and the SPIDER framework to explore Canva’s role in secondary education, focusing on its uses, benefits and challenges. From 1,725 initial records, 15 peer-reviewed studies ,lastly from Indonesia and a few from Malaysia met the inclusion criteria. Findings show that Canva is widely used for visual learning and content creation in language, social studies and science subjects. It enhances student motivation, comprehension, creativity, improves writing and digital literacy. However, its classroom use remains short-term and teacher-centered , with limited focus on science and higher-order thinking. Reported challenges include low digital literacy, poor infrastructure and insufficient teacher training. Overall, Canva is a flexible platform that supports 21st-century learning, but equitable access and teacher readiness are essential for its effective technology integration.

items.title: From Likes to Logic: Explainable Machine Learning for Higher-Education Social Media Engagement
items.abstract: Social media is used by higher educational institutions in order to communicate, build their reputations, recruit students, engage in stakeholder relations and engage with the public. Machine learning can predict post-level engagement by analyzing features and characteristics of the content, time, platform, sentiment, and interaction metrics; however, the ability to predict doesn't account for why a post is likely to be successful. This review brings together recent literature on social media engagement in higher education; machine learning prediction of social media engagement; and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) research from related disciplines in education, highlighting the disconnect between higher education social media engagement research and XAI research occurring in neighboring higher education fields. The literature is categorized into three classes according to the target of engagement, the modality of the data, the platform, the model family, and the explanation strategy. Content and plat-form context are shown to be lasting factors, while cross-platform generalization, multimodal representation, temporal robustness, causal interpretation, and ex-planation quality are all shown to be under-developed. A conceptual workflow is synthesized from the source presentation and existing literature spanning from the data collection to the data preprocessing, feature selection, model training, prediction, explanation, and decision support. The research agenda emerging from these focuses on time-aware validation, multi-institution datasets, semantic and multimodal features, stable and human-centric explanations, causal evaluation, and responsible data governance. The outline is designed as a reference architecture based on the review, not as a report of the experimental results that have been acquired.

items.title: From Research Gaps to Theoretical Opportunities: Theory-Oriented GenAI for Research Opportunity Evaluation
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) can explore large bodies of literature and generate plausible research ideas, but identifying what is missing, understudied, contradictory, or potentially connected does not by itself reveal where theory should advance. We develop a theory-oriented agentic AI system that helps researchers identify potential theorizing opportunities by incorporating established theorizing approaches into literature exploration and evaluation. The system operates through three stages. Stage 1 expands the theoretical search space and constructs a provisional Candidate Knowledge Graph. Stage 2 independently reconstructs what the literature supports through source grounded evidence extraction and theory-state reconstruction. Stage 3 evaluates the reconstructed knowledge state to determine whether an unresolved configuration warrants theory development or another research action and, when theory development is warranted, which theorizing approach is appropriate. We demonstrate the system through an end-to-end analysis of human oversight of agentic AI systems in organizations. The analysis shows that literature gaps alone are insufficient for identifying theoretical opportunities. For example, "transparency to trust" is routed to mechanism-based theorizing because the relationship is repeatedly documented in prior studies, while the generative mechanism explaining how transparency shapes trust remains insufficiently specified. By combining large-scale literature processing, structured knowledge representation, and theorizing-guided diagnosis, the system serves as a theory-oriented research assistant that supports researchers in identifying theoretically meaningful directions for subsequent research.

items.title: From Saliency Maps to Circuits: An Integrative Survey of Explainable AI and Mechanistic Interpretability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models, particularly those based on deep learning, have achieved strong performance across a wide range of real-world applications. However, as models increase in scale and complexity, their behavior and internal decision-making processes become increasingly difficult to understand. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has emerged to address this challenge by developing methods for making model predictions and internal mechanisms more transparent and intelligible. Despite substantial progress, the XAI landscape remains difficult to navigate due to methodological diversity, inconsistent terminology, and increasingly distinct research directions. In particular, classical XAI techniques, which primarily explain model predictions and behavior, and mechanistic interpretability (MI), which seeks to understand internal representations and computations, are often studied separately. This paper provides an integrative survey of these approaches, bringing them together within a shared taxonomy that spans explanatory scope, stage, and methodological foundations. The review examines their underlying principles, assumptions, strengths, and limitations while also surveying evaluation criteria for assessing explanation quality and highlighting connections and distinctions across the broader interpretability landscape. By synthesizing these research directions within a common framework, the study aims to provide a cohesive reference for understanding, organizing, and comparing methods for explaining machine learning models.

items.title: From Social Reasoning to Embodied Interaction: An Agentic Framework for Social Robots
items.abstract: Natural face-to-face human--robot interaction requires a robot to understand an evolving social situation, decide when to engage, and express its intent through coordinated physical behavior. Yet existing approaches rarely close this loop: foundation-model agents provide increasingly capable multimodal reasoning and memory but remain largely disembodied, while expressive virtual agents do not face the physical constraints of real robots, and physical social robots typically address social reasoning and embodied expression only partially. We present ARISE, a unified framework that bridges Agentic Reasoning and Interactive Social Embodiment on the Sophia humanoid robot. ARISE integrates multimodal context understanding, long-term memory, and reactive and proactive interaction to determine when and what to communicate, and translates social intent into robot-native gestures coordinated with speech and mechanical facial expressions through streaming execution. Extensive evaluations on Sophia demonstrate strong perceived interaction quality, expressive and well-coordinated embodied behavior, and substantial latency reductions through streaming execution. These results highlight the importance of jointly reasoning about what to communicate, when to engage, and how to physically express social intent for natural interaction with humanoid robots. items.title: From Token-Max to Outcome-Max: How You Use AI Determines Its Productivity
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) models can perform increasingly complex tasks, yet greater AI usage does not necessarily translate into proportional productivity gains. We identify token-max as one source of this inefficiency: when token consumption is treated as productive effort, agents are encouraged to over-exert and expend computation beyond what is necessary. We instead propose outcome-max, which rewards independently verified task completion per unit cost and induces a principled stopping rule. Then, to study these objectives, we develop a three-level simulation framework spanning immediate interaction, long-run behavioral adaptation, and organizational collaboration. Across all three levels, outcome-max improves the efficiency of AI-assisted production while largely preserving verified task performance. To further align these incentives with outcome-max, we introduce OutcomeShare, an incentive mechanism. Theory and simulation show that OutcomeShare can induce participation while generating shared gains for employees, firms, and LLM providers. Together, our results suggest that AI productivity not only depends on model capability, but also on how to construct the objectives governing AI use.

items.title: From Trust-by-Design to Continuous Trust in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Trust is crucial in the digital world, particularly in the age of systems based on artificial intelligence. Traditionally, system correctness is demonstrated by proving that the system satisfies the required properties. However, digital systems involve humans, who can make mistakes, break rules, or even intentionally cheat the system. Technical devices may also malfunction or cause errors. Therefore, external stakeholders need to trust a system throughout its operation. To address this challenge, we propose the concept of continuous trust. In this paper, we present a detailed explanation of this concept, based on a running example of a business's refund department. The paper concludes with a discussion of related work, such as compliance checking and certification, as well as an outlook on further questions regarding the formalization and the necessary tool support.

items.title: Gentle Algorithms and Educational Relationships
items.abstract: When AI learns to imitate the way your favorite teacher, deceased relative, or ex-partner speaks, it can offer unconditional gentle responses—but is this gentleness genuine companionship or a refined substitution? Artificial intelligence emotional simulation learns the tone, attitude, and response patterns of specific others through data, providing students with stable and controllable emotional support. It may alleviate loneliness, yet it may also replace real others with simulacra, hollowing out educational relationships. Existing research oscillates between technological optimism and ethical critique, overlooking the conditionality of its educational consequences. Drawing on relational ethics, simulacra theory, and educational phenomenology, this paper develops a "supplementary–substitutional" analytical framework, examining its impact along four dimensions: degree of substitution, transparency, exitability, and subject generation. It argues that AI emotional simulation is neither intrinsically good nor bad: under supplementary, transparent, exit-friendly conditions that serve subject generation, it can become a resource for educational emotional support; only under conditions that replace real others, operate covertly, preclude exit, and dissolve subject generation does it constitute an ethical dilemma. The discussion shifts from "judgments of good or bad" to "analysis of conditions," providing a theoretical tool for research on educational relationships and AI ethics.

items.title: Governing Agentic AI in Healthcare: A Systematic Review of Autonomous Decision-Making, Clinical Safety, and Public Accountability
items.abstract: Background Agentic artificial intelligence systems capable of autonomous reasoning, planning, tool invocation, and clinical action are entering health services faster than existing governance instruments can accommodate. Whether empirical evaluations document the institutional arrangements these systems require has not been systematically examined across clinical domains. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched OpenAlex, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore on 8 September 2026 for empirical studies of agentic artificial intelligence in clinical tasks, benchmarks, and deployment settings. Eligibility under the SPIDER framework required a clinical sample and evidence in the full text of at least three of four agentic capabilities: multi-step reasoning, planning, runtime tool-calling, and autonomous execution. Accountability findings reflect documentation within empirical evaluations rather than legal or regulatory literature. Two reviewers independently screened 1,793 records and assessed 81 full texts, with all eligibility disagreements formally adjudicated against source texts. Appraisal used a custom eight-domain codebook. Extraction covered 24 fields across four research questions addressing architecture, clinical safety, safeguards, and accountability. Results Fifty-two studies met inclusion criteria; 34 peer reviewed, 18 preprints, 32 from 2026. Across the predefined reporting domains, documentation was highest for architecture (96 per cent) and progressively less frequent for clinical safety (78 per cent), safeguards (62 per cent), and accountability (28 per cent). Vendor accountability and patient contestability each appeared in one study, workforce impact in three. Adversarial security was evaluated in five studies. Twenty-seven of 52 studies did not report a fail-safe protocol. Conclusions The evidence base describes agentic clinical systems in architectural detail and increasingly in safety terms, but provides limited empirical documentation of procurement standards, liability allocation, workforce assessment, and patient recourse. Safety evaluation and accountability instrumentation answer different questions, and closing the second is not a by-product of improving the first.

items.title: Grounded Joint-Attention Other-Play for Zero-Shot Coordination
items.abstract: Joint attention - the human ability to share a common visual or cognitive focus with others - enables a meeting of minds that lets us coordinate even with unfamiliar partners. In this work we investigate whether equipping AI agents with a similar mechanism can enable such zero-shot coordination. We introduce Mutual Attention for zero-shot TEaming (MATE): a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning method inspired by human joint attention. MATE encourages agents to coordinate their actions by aligning their visual attention on scene-salient objects during the interaction rather than relying on arbitrary partner-dependent conventions established during training. Unlike symmetry-breaking approaches that merely prevent brittle conventions from emerging, MATE actively promotes coordination through an environment-grounded signal that is naturally shared across partners. We evaluate MATE on three benchmarks: our Card Alignment Game, designed to isolate brittle convention formation, and the more challenging Level-Based Foraging and OvercookedV2 benchmarks. Our experiments consistently show that a joint-attention-inspired signal improves coordination with unknown partners, underlining MATE's potential as a general coordination mechanism that complements and surpasses symmetry-breaking approaches.

items.title: HACCP for AI: An Auditable Self-Control Standard for Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Almost every serious instrument in AI governance now requires an organisation to run a risk process. None of them tells the organisation where in its own lifecycle the control points sit, what measurable limit applies at each one, what happens automatically when a limit is breached, or who is competent to verify the measurement. That layer, process control, is missing, and it is the layer on which everything else depends. A management system without control points produces documentation; it does not produce safety. This paper supplies that layer by importing a method that has governed an invisible hazard across a globally distributed production chain for more than fifty years: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. The claim is deliberately narrow. HACCP is not proposed as a rival to ISO/IEC 42001, to Article 9 of the EU AI Act, or to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It is proposed as the process-control layer their architecture presupposes and does not contain, and as the one methodology in existence with a property AI governance urgently needs and currently lacks: scale invariance. The same seven principles govern a village bakery and a multinational dairy, which is why one inspector, one standard and one accreditation system can cover both. The method is given in the full twelve-step Codex sequence, with a three-tier proportionality rule, deployer, provider, frontier developer, a hazard taxonomy, a control-point decision tree, a catalogue of seven control points, and a taxonomy of limits that separates critical limits from operational limits and indicator thresholds, and reclassifies the compute thresholds now written into law as the third kind. Version 5.0 supplied the instruments: attribute sampling plans with their operating characteristics, statistical process control that gives the operational limit an exact meaning, a seven-step protocol for validating an evaluation as a measuring instrument, and record schemas that make version identity and traceability a matter of implementation. Version 6.0 adds what September 2026 asked for. At the United Nations Security Council the heads of the two largest frontier laboratories called for external evaluators embedded with employee-like access, "similar to a food inspector"; for common standards so that countries can compare evidence and verify compliance; for incident classification and reporting protocols; for a way to measure and pace the automation of AI research; and for standards that preserve meaningful human oversight. Food law has settled forms for each, and this version writes them into the plan: the resident inspector, with the eleven properties the September proposals ask for read against the articles of the European official-controls regulation that already provide them, an inspection record, and a funding model that makes independence enforceable rather than promised; a four-level incident severity scale built on recorded facts, with the statutory clocks in force; the pre-registered safety case as the condition of a training run; measurable pace indicators for self-improvement with slowing and pausing as written corrective actions; and the planted error, the metal-detector test piece of food lines, as the measure of whether human review is real. The instruments of Part II are updated to the 2026 evaluation literature, including evaluation awareness as a threat to validity, and the year's five public incidents are read as deviations, each with the record that would have been required next. The paper states its own limits without softening. The most consequential gap in AI-governance infrastructure is metrological: there is no analogue of ISO/IEC 17025 for capability evaluation, and until there is, independent attestation of a capability-based limit is not available to anyone. One structural disanalogy has no food-safety precedent at all: a pathogen does not model the control system trying to detect it, and a sufficiently capable AI system may. Both are treated as design constraints on the method rather than as objections to be answered later. The framework is accordingly strongest where most AI harm occurs, in organisations that deploy and provide AI systems, and is stated to be aspirational at the frontier until independent measurement exists; the resident inspector is the part of it a frontier laboratory can adopt this year, because its independence can be accredited before its measurements can. This record contains three files: the full paper (version 6.0, 86 pages), a two-page Executive Summary for policy readers, and a 20-page Practitioner Brief containing Part II (the instruments) as a standalone document. Version 6.0 supersedes version 5.0.1 (September 2026); earlier versions remain available under the same concept DOI. CC BY 4.0.

items.title: How AI-Generated Language Shapes User Trust in Social Media? A Systematic Review
items.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed social media communication by enabling AI systems to produce increasingly human-like language and content. Although research on AI-generated communication and user trust has expanded, findings remain fragmented across platforms, communication contexts, and linguistic characteristics. This study systematically synthesizes empirical evidence on the relationship between AI-generated language and user trust in social media communication. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Literature was retrieved from the Dimensions database in July 2026 using predefined search terms related to Generative AI, language, trust, and social media. Of 205 records initially identified, 54 full-text studies were assessed for eligibility, and 23 empirical studies were included in the final synthesis. The findings show that research is concentrated in recent years, particularly in marketing and digital communication, health communication, and misinformation and synthetic media. Across the studies, trust is associated with recurring linguistic and communicative features, including human-likeness and conversational style, emotional expression and empathy, personalization, formality and readability, narrative and experiential language, semantic and informational characteristics, transparency and disclosure, and explanatory language. The findings indicate that user trust is not determined by AI authorship alone but emerges through the interaction of relational and epistemic cues within specific communication contexts. This review contributes to human–AI communication research by identifying linguistic and communicative mechanisms through which AI-generated social media content shapes perceptions of trust, credibility, and authenticity.

items.title: Impact of generative AI on Teaching and Learning Processes
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has become a highly transformative technology with the capacity to reshape teaching and learning in schools and other educational institutions.Since it can facilitate intelligent content generation, adaptive learning, automated assessment, and personalized instructional support, Generative AI provides numerous opportunities for improving the quality of education, increasing learner engagement, and boosting instructional efficiency.This paper gives a critical look at the effect of Generative AI on teaching and learning by looking at its applications, advantages, challenges, and future potential in the education sector.The study looks at major opportunities such as personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, content creation, and collaborative learning environments, while also tackling important issues like algorithmic opacity, explainability, data privacy and security, bias and fairness, academic integrity, and the reliability of content produced by AI.The paper also examines ways of responsibly introducing Generative AI by creating transparent and ethical AI frameworks, establishing strong data governance mechanisms, setting up appropriate regulatory policies, and using high-quality training datasets.It stresses the need to give teachers the necessary AI skills through ongoing professional development so that they can effectively incorporate AI-based teaching methods.Lastly, the study highlights some of the new trends in AI-driven education, such as intelligent tutoring systems, immersive virtual learning environments, adaptive assessment, and collaborative human-AI learning ecosystems.The results show that although Generative AI offers great potential for enhancing educational accessibility, personalization, and learning outcomes, its successful implementation relies on ethical governance, responsible use, and continued cooperation between educators, researchers, policymakers, and technology developers.

items.abstract: Abstrak: Kegiatan pengabdian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh kebutuhan penguatan kompetensi digital guru sekolah dasar serta kebutuhan alternatif pembelajaran yang lebih fleksibel pada sekolah mitra yang menghadapi gangguan pembelajaran akibat banjir musiman. Kegiatan bertujuan meningkatkan kompetensi digital guru melalui implementasi LMS LENTERA 101752 serta pelatihan pengembangan media berbantuan Generative AI dan Augmented Reality (AR). Kegiatan dilaksanakan melalui pelatihan dan workshop dengan mitra guruSD Negeri di, Kabupaten Deli Serdang, yang melibatkan 21 guru. Evaluasi dilakukan melalui observasi selama kegiatan serta pre-test dan post-test kompetensi digital. Data pre-test dan post-test dianalisis secara deskriptif dengan membandingkan nilai rata-rata sebelum dan sesudah kegiatan, menghitung selisih peningkatan nilai dan persentase peningkatan, serta menentukan proporsi peserta yang mengalami peningkatan nilai Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan rata-rata nilai meningkat dari 62,11 menjadi 82,63 atau meningkat 20,53 poin (33,05%) dengan N-gain 0,54 (kategori sedang) dan 94,74% peserta mengalami peningkatan nilai. Kegiatan memberikan progres positif terhadap kompetensi digital guru dalam memanfaatkan LMS, Generative AI, dan AR untuk mendukung pengembangan pembelajaran yang lebih fleksibel dan interaktif.Abstract: This community engagement program was motivated by the need to strengthen elementary school teachers’ digital competence and provide more flexible learning alternatives in a partner school affected by seasonal flooding. The program aimed to improve teachers’ digital competence through the implementation of the LENTERA 101752 Learning Management System (LMS) and training in developing learning media using Generative AI and Augmented Reality (AR). The activities were conducted through training and workshops involving 21 teachers from a public elementary school in Deli Serdang Regency. Evaluation was conducted through observation during the activities, as well as pre-test and post-test assessments of teachers’ digital competence. The data were analyzed descriptively by comparing the mean scores before and after the activities, calculating the difference and percentage increase, and determining the proportion of participants whose scores improved. The evaluation results showed that the mean score increased from 62.11 to 82.63, representing an increase of 20.53 points (33.05%), with an N-gain of 0.54 (moderate category), and 94.74% of participants showing an improvement in their scores. The program demonstrated positive progress in teachers’ digital competence in utilizing LMS, Generative AI, and AR to support more flexible and interactive learning.

items.title: Improving human performance in deepfake detection: limits of aggregation and human–AI collaboration
items.abstract: Abstract Given that deepfake videos are now easy to generate and increasingly high in quality, the present research investigated human detection performance and several routes to improvement. Across four experiments, participants demonstrated above-chance detection accuracy when viewing YouTube clips and their corresponding deepfakes, but performance remained modest and error-prone. In Experiment 1, aggregating responses across the full sample produced reliable improvements in accuracy, consistent with a ‘wisdom of the crowd’ effect. However, in Experiment 2, participants showed no evidence of metacognitive sensitivity. Although confidence was modestly higher for correct than incorrect decisions, it did not reliably discriminate between them at the trial level. Consistent with this finding, confidence-weighted fusion of participant pairs reduced rather than improved accuracy. In Experiments 3 and 4, we examined human–AI collaboration, with participants making decisions before and after receiving simulated algorithmic guidance. Performance improved following guidance when it was highly accurate, but this benefit was offset by a tendency to follow incorrect advice when it occurred. Notably, this reliance on simulated algorithmic guidance was unaffected by the prevalence of deepfakes within the stimulus set. Taken together, these findings suggest that, while both aggregation and human–AI collaboration can enhance performance under certain conditions, their effectiveness is constrained by poor metacognitive insight and a general tendency to align decisions with external advice. Improving deepfake detection may depend not only on advances in algorithmic performance, but also on a better understanding of how humans interpret and use both perceptual and algorithmic information.

items.title: Improving Mathematics Interest through Problem-Solving Strategy: Evidence from Senior Secondary Students
items.abstract: This study investigated the impact of a problem-solving instructional strategy on the interest of senior secondary school students in mathematics in Kaduna State, Nigeria. Rooted in Self-Determination Theory, which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as drivers of intrinsic motivation, the research employed a quasi-experimental pre-test, post-test control group design. A total of 204 SS2 students from three public schools were assigned to either an experimental group, which was taught using a structured problem-solving strategy, or a control group, which was instructed via conventional methods. Students’ interest in mathematics was assessed using a validated adaptation of the Mathematics Interest Questionnaire (MIQ). Data were analysed using ANCOVA to control for baseline differences. Results indicated a statistically significant positive effect of the problem-solving strategy on students’ post-test interest scores (F(1, 130) = 13.590, p < .001, η² = .095), affirming the hypothesis that learner-centred, inquiry-driven instruction fosters greater affective engagement than traditional approaches. These findings underscore the role of problem-solving in stimulating psychological engagement and enhancing the affective domain in mathematics learning. The study contributes to the broader literature advocating for pedagogical reforms that prioritise active learning, especially within under-resourced and socio-culturally diverse educational contexts. Implications for theory, policy, and instructional practice are discussed, alongside recommendations for future research into long-term and demographic-specific effects of problem-solving pedagogy.

items.abstract: This research investigates the impact of artificial intelligence on contemporary training systems, emphasizing its function in providing individualized learning, increasing interest in tasks, and offering instantaneous feedback. Lastly, the author presents suggestions for organizational policies that wish to incorporate AI technologies into training programs in a manner that responsibly prepares them for future workplace challenges.

items.title: Integrating virtual reality into engineering education: Experimental study of differential leveling in surveying
items.abstract: Hands-on training is essential in surveying education, where students must develop both conceptual understanding and procedural accuracy in tasks such as differential leveling. Traditional field-based instruction is often constrained by limited equipment, logistical challenges, and restricted opportunities for repeated practice. Virtual reality (VR) offers a scalable alternative, yet prior work has largely focused on system development with limited empirical evaluation of performance and learning outcomes. This study presents the design and evaluation of a VR-based laboratory for teaching differential leveling, integrating immersive interaction, real-time feedback, and realistic task simulation. A controlled study with engineering students assessed learning outcomes, task performance, usability, cognitive workload, and user experience. Results show improvements in post-task learning, indicating gains in both procedural and conceptual understanding. Participants reported high usability, strong engagement, and low frustration. Log data revealed consistent procedural execution but greater difficulty in later-stage calculations, particularly foresight and elevation computation, partly due to limited familiarity with metric leveling staff readings. Statistical analysis showed that inaccurate participants required significantly more interactions and that interaction count was strongly correlated with completion time, while error rates differed significantly across task components. However, interaction frequency was not significantly associated with total error count, suggesting that interaction effort and task accuracy capture distinct dimensions of learner performance. These findings suggest that VR-based laboratories can effectively support surveying education by enabling structured practice, identifying learning challenges, and reinforcing key concepts in a controlled environment.

items.title: Lesson Plans for Assessment and Test Construction in Social Sciences Education: Integrating Classical and Modern Approaches with Human-AI Integration (HAI)
items.abstract: This educational resource comprises a complete set of 12 lesson plans and accompanying handouts for a course titled "Assessment and Test Construction in Social Sciences Education". The course is designed for third-semester pre-service teachers at Farhangian University, Iran, and is delivered in Persian. The course adopts a blended approach, integrating classical assessment paradigms (e.g., Classical Test Theory, Bloom's Taxonomy, Cronbach's Alpha, Messick's validity framework) with modern AI-era perspectives (e.g., Integrated AI Triad (IAT), Reverse PCK, Comparative Adjudication Protocol (CAP), Toolprint, Consistency Quotient (CQ), AI-Resistant Tasks, and TVDT). A central innovation is the Human-AI Integration (HAI) framework, which positions AI as a co-thinker rather than a replacement for teacher judgment. The 12 sessions guide students through a complete assessment cycle, from foundational concepts to the design, validation, and publication of a comprehensive assessment package. Each session includes a handout (classical and/or integrated), a lesson plan with operational prompts, and a team-based project milestone. By the end of the course, each team produces a six-component assessment package for a selected lesson from Sociology 1 or 2, and publishes it as an open educational resource on Zenodo. The 12 Sessions Fundamental Concepts of Assessment and the Learning-Assessment Life Cycle – Distinguishing measurement, assessment, evaluation, and test; introducing the six-stage learning-assessment cycle. Classification of Tests and Knowledge Graph – Classical test classification (Sif's ten perspectives); extracting the knowledge graph of a lesson; identifying blind spots and error scenarios. Two-Dimensional Table and Consistency Quotient (CQ) – Designing a Bloom × content table; calculating CQ to measure internal coherence. Attitude Assessment and Task Vulnerability Diagnostic Triad (TVDT) – Likert scales and reliability; analyzing task vulnerability using TVDT. Item Bank and Cognitive Depth (Toolprint) – Bloom's taxonomy and item analysis; introducing Toolprint (Interrogative Density, Interrogative Range, Tool Alignment). Validity, Reliability, and Comparative Adjudication Protocol (CAP) – CVR, CVI, Cronbach's Alpha; CAP for resolving inter-rater discrepancies. Statistical Analysis of Tests – Classical Test Theory (p, D, item-total correlation) and Item Response Theory (IRT); data-driven analysis with AI. Growth-Oriented Feedback – Hattie & Timperley's three-question model; AI-generated feedback patterns; compassionate feedback. Performance Assessment and Rubric – Authentic assessment and analytic rubrics; AI-Resistant Tasks and four resistance mechanisms. Digital Assessment Infrastructure and Targeted Remediation – Portfolios and digital infrastructure; three-layer remedial redesign (PRC Workshop). Norm-Referenced Tests – Norms, Z-scores, T-scores, stanines; smart norms and computerized adaptive testing (CAT). Presenting the Assessment Package and Publishing in Zenodo – Classical reporting vs. open dissemination; preparing the package for Zenodo with DOI. Intended Audience Teacher educators, pre-service social science teachers, curriculum designers, and researchers in educational assessment. Course Structure 26 teams, each working on one lesson from Sociology 1 or 2 (27 lessons total). Team roles: Documentation Manager (laptop access), Prompt Engineer (AI account control), Qualitative Evaluator (output review). All lesson plans and handouts are in Persian.

items.title: Let the Agent Do It? How Software Practitioners Understand and Make Permission Decisions in Agentic AI Assistants
items.abstract: Agentic AI assistants increasingly act on developers' behalf by modifying files, executing commands, and accessing external resources. These actions often require permission, yet little is known about how practitioners make permission decisions while still benefiting from agent autonomy. To address this gap, we conducted a sequential mixed methods study, interviewing 18 practitioners who use AI agents and then surveying 115 practitioners based on the interview findings. We find that practitioners often understand agent behaviour through what they can directly observe and review, while decisions, data use, and other activity behind the scenes remain less clear. This uncertainty also shapes permission decisions, which depend on the scope and risk of an action, whether it fits the task, familiarity with the agent, and the environment in which it operates. Practitioners respond by adjusting how closely they oversee agents, from setting limits in advance to monitoring execution and reviewing work afterwards. How much scrutiny they apply depends on factors such as trust, task importance, time pressure, and the consequences of an action. Our findings suggest that permission systems should make consequential actions easier to review, distinguish what an agent is allowed to do from what the user intended, make reversibility clearer, avoid treating repeated approvals as stable preferences, and distinguish rejecting a single action from rejecting an entire approach.

items.title: Living with Risk: Folk Theories of AI Hallucinations Among Young Chinese Users
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life, AI hallucinations have emerged as a significant challenge in human-AI interaction. Drawing on the perspective of algorithmic folk theories, this study combines textual analysis and in-depth interviews with both ordinary users and technical users to examine how they understand and respond to AI hallucinations. Users identify AI hallucinations by scrutinizing the AI’s reasoning process, making intuitive judgments, and conducting cross-validation, while their attitudes toward hallucinations vary. Users develop four types of algorithmic folk theories: the Human-AI Interaction Misalignment Theory, the Technical Limitations Theory, the Data Source Distortion Theory, and the Generative Rule Constraint Theory. They rise to four corresponding coping strategies: reducing communication errors, reconfiguring human-AI task allocation, intervening in data input while verifying outputs, and reducing AI’s processing load. This study further indicates how technological identity and sociotechnical contexts jointly shape algorithmic folk theories.

items.title: Mathematical modeling of muscle fatigue recovery time for drilling operations
items.abstract: Workers exposed to hand-transmitted vibration are at high risk of developing musculoskeletal disorders due to excessive muscle fatigue, and prolonged vibration exposure impairs the ability to recover effectively. Effective work design, including adequate rest intervals, is essential to minimize fatigue accumulation and its effects. This study evaluated the influence of four drilling parameters on muscle fatigue recovery time (MFRT) and developed a predictive mathematical model. The parameters investigated were drilling duration, feed force, material hardness, and drill bit diameter, each tested at two levels. A randomized complete block design was employed, with 16 treatment combinations replicated thrice. Participants were randomly assigned to treatment combinations. The MFRT was defined as the duration for muscle electrical activation to reach 80% of its initial maximum voluntary EMG Root Mean Square (RMS) value. The RMS value of the EMG was normalized using the amplitude analysis function and presented as a percentage of the maximum voluntary contraction. The results show significant impacts of feed force, drilling duration, and material hardness on MFRT, increasing it by 64.28%, 64.2%, and 22.78%, respectively. The two-factor interactions between feed force and material hardness, as well as duration and material hardness, were significant, while the three-factor interaction between feed force, duration, and material hardness also significantly impacted MFRT. The predictive model developed was validated by comparing experimental data with the model predictions. This study's findings can guide the optimization of drilling work design to ensure sufficient recovery time, thereby reducing the risk of musculoskeletal disorders among workers.

items.title: Measuring AI literacy in design education: development and validation of the artificial intelligence literacy scale for design students
items.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in design practice, challenging how design education fosters students’ AI literacy and thus prepares students to engage efficiently with AI. However, there is currently no domain-specific theoretical framework and reliable instrument in the literature to conceptualize and assess design students’ AI literacy, hindering its systematic cultivation. This study fills in this gap by developing and validating the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale for Design Students (AILS-DS), in accordance with established standards for scale development. The opinions of a wide range of experts were gathered through a qualitative method in order to define the AI literacy for design students, and served as a theoretical framework for the scale’s item pool. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA, N = 294) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA, N = 325) were then applied to explore the underlying factor structure of the scale and validate its psychometric properties. The final 23-item, five-factor scale demonstrated good reliability and construct validity. Five factors (AI Concepts and Technical Skills, AI Tool Proficiency, AI Ethics and Originality Awareness, Recognition of AI Value in Design, and Independent Evaluation of AI Outputs) in the AILS-DS capture both widely acknowledged AI literacy components and design-specific structure, reflecting the designerly way of knowing and thinking. This study provides a practical tool for educators and researchers, supporting the assessment and cultivation of AI literacy in design education and laying a foundation for pedagogical innovation in the AI era.

items.title: MedPrune: Topology-Efficient Multimodal Multi-Agent Communication Evolution for Medical VQA Tasks
items.abstract: While medical multimodal large language models (Med-MLLMs) advance medical visual question answering (VQA), existing clinical workflow-inspired multi-agent frameworks suffer from interaction patterns and excessive computational overhead caused by redundant communication topologies. In this paper, we propose MedPrune, an efficient medical multimodal multi-agent collaboration framework that dynamically prunes both nodes and edges from the communication topology to enhance reasoning ability and token efficiency. Specifically, we first formulate the diagnostic process as a heterogeneous communication graph, where nodes represent specialist agents from various departments and edges capture intra- and inter-departmental interactions. Building on this graph, we introduce two sparsification mechanisms to enable adaptive collaborative evolution: (1) Heterogeneous Node Sparsification, which eliminates task-irrelevant specialist agents irrelevant to the current multimodal question via reinforcement learning-driven topological optimization, and (2) Heterogeneous Edge Sparsification, which selectively retains only the most diagnostically salient intra- and inter-departmental connections by jointly optimizing task performance and topological complexity. Extensive medical VQA experiments under full-set and few-shot training settings prove MedPrune surpasses multi-agent baselines and boosts token efficiency with strong adversarial robustness.

items.title: Meta-synthesis of global cases for the adaption stages of artificial intelligence systems into university practices
items.abstract: Abstract The transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in universities is simply extending beyond instructional applications to include administrative and strategic domains in university management. This study aims to explore how AI could be integrated into university practices by addressing three core questions: to what AI technologies are being employed, which integration stages support their implementation, and what kind of ethical risks need to be considered for AI usage in universities. To respond to these questions, the researchers a meta-synthesis approach to qualitatively analyse selected studies. Based on a systematic search protocol, they selected 49 empirical cases from different parts of the world; then, analysed them using thematic analysis through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing/verification. The findings were categorised into a three-layered framework capturing various purposes of AI usage, technical and institutional integration steps, and the components of ethical AI regulations in universities. The analysis shows that higher education authorities, university leaders, and techno-experts initially decide the purpose(s) of AI usage, regarding teaching, research, engagement, and administration. Then, as a structured roadmap, they can follow eight steps identified for the technical and institutional AI integration: 1. AI System Design, 2. AI Algorithm Development, 3. Data Management-Preprocessing, 4. AI System Integration, 5. Strategic Management Policies, 6. Operational Management Roles, 7. Curriculum-Pedagogical Design, and 8. Evaluation-Performance Monitoring. Lastly, ethical regulations could be organised combining sub-themes of Data Ethics, Algorithmic Ethics, Human-AI Interaction and Social Impact, Academic Integrity and Responsible Use, and Institutional and Managerial Ethics.

items.title: Metaverse and generative AI in education: a scoping review of technologies, applications, evaluation, challenges, and future directions
items.abstract: The convergence of Metaverse technologies and Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping immersive digital education. This study presents a scoping review of Metaverse and GenAI-enabled education following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. A systematic search of ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink identified 114 primary studies published or indexed from January 2022 up to the respective database search dates in 2026. Based on the synthesized evidence, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy that classifies existing research across application domains, Metaverse technologies, GenAI categories, target user groups, degrees of freedom (DoF), pedagogical foundations, evaluation practices, technical limitations, and future research directions. The reviewed studies show that Virtual Reality (VR) is the predominant immersive modality (61%), while OpenAI-based models represent the most widely adopted GenAI ecosystem (60%). Applications are concentrated primarily in STEM, higher education, and healthcare, where immersive learning environments increasingly incorporate intelligent tutoring, adaptive feedback, virtual agents, and automated content generation. Although 68% (77 articles) of the reviewed studies reported user perceptual evaluations, these predominantly focused on short-term usability and engagement, with comparatively limited attention to longitudinal learning effectiveness, knowledge retention, cognitive outcomes, AI trustworthiness, accessibility, inclusivity, and real-world deployment. This imbalance reveals a central maturity gap: technological sophistication is advancing faster than the educational evidence needed to establish sustained learning effectiveness and real-world readiness. Commonly reported challenges include limited empirical validation, system maturity, scalability, interoperability, AI trustworthiness, immersive performance, accessibility, and ethical governance. Based on these findings, we identify key priorities for future research, including longitudinal and pedagogically grounded evaluation, scalable and interoperable system architectures, trustworthy AI, inclusive and ecologically valid validation, and stronger integration of pedagogical and governance considerations. The proposed taxonomy provides an evidence-based framework to support future research, comparative analysis, and the design of Metaverse and GenAI-enabled educational systems.

items.title: Motivação, estimativa de desempenho e o rendimento físico de estudantes do ensino médio
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The level of motivation for engaging in physical activity and exercise varies among individuals and may be influenced by psychological and social factors.OBJECTIVE: To assess motivation, prior estimates of own performance, and physical performance among high school boys and girls.METHODS: A total of 124 students (67 boys, 16.16±1.10 years; and 57 girls, 16.42±1.50 years) enrolled in technical programs integrated into high school at two public schools within the Federal Education Network participated in the study. Physical activity level (IPAQ) and motivation to engage in physical exercise (BREQ-2) were assessed. Before the physical tests, participants numerically estimated the performance they expected to achieve in the medicine ball throw, 20-m speed test, agility test, horizontal jump, and push-up test. The absolute difference between the actual and estimated values was used to quantify the magnitude of discrepancies between these values (Absolute Estimation Error—AEE).RESULTS: Boys presented higher levels of intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, and self-determination of motivation. In the medicine ball throw, horizontal jump, and push-up tests, actual performance was, on average, higher than estimated, whereas in the 20-m speed and agility tests, actual times were lower than estimated, for both boys and girls. AEE was lower among girls in the medicine ball throw and push-up tests and among boys in the 20-m speed and agility tests. No sex difference was observed in the horizontal jump.CONCLUSION: In this study, boys presented a more self-determined motivational profile than girls. The discrepancy between estimated and actual performance varied according to the test, and AEE differed between sexes in four of the five tests.
